responses.rationale: The helper clearly builds a non-literal RegExp from its regex parameter, so the dynamic-pattern sink is present. The excerpt does not show any caller, registration of this function as a SQL UDF, or whether either argument can come from untrusted input. Without source and attacker-control evidence, exploitability cannot be established or ruled out.

A hardcoded apiKey string is present in client-facing Docusaurus Algolia config. The packet does not establish whether this key is a privileged secret, a deliberately public search-only key, or used for any server-side privileged operation. Without privilege and secrecy evidence, an actionable secret-leak conclusion is not defensible.

Although a dynamic RegExp is constructed, searchFilter is first escaped with a metacharacter replacement, so user-supplied search text is treated as a literal substring rather than an attacker-controlled pattern. The claimed unsafe non-literal-regexp path is blocked by that escaping.

SQL text is assembled from a fixed id predicate with a placeholder; the identifier is bound via args to ExecContext, not interpolated into the query string. String joining of constant WHERE fragments does not establish SQL injection.

The method signs a caller-supplied payload as a JWT and optionally encrypts it when encryption_key is set. The packet does not show what claims are placed in the payload, whether they are sensitive, or whether callers always encrypt. Presence of JWT encoding alone does not establish exposed sensitive data.
The DELETE statement concatenates only the fixed predicate id = $1; the ID is supplied as a bound argument. No user-controlled SQL fragment is shown.
SET and WHERE clauses use fixed SQL with $1/$2 placeholders; status and ID are passed in args to QueryRowContext. Values are not concatenated into the SQL text.

verified_dimensions.mitigation: fixed assignments and predicate with bound args

responses.rationale: The excerpt only shows pickle.dumps when writing schedule fields. The dangerous sink for this rule class is untrusted deserialization, which is not present here. Serialization alone is not an operationally actionable exploit path from this evidence.

pickle.loads on stored args, kwargs, and options is a real deserialization sink and is used on the schedule dispatch path. The packet does not show who can create or modify those stored bytes, so attacker control of the pickle blob cannot be established. A defensible confirmed or mitigated decision requires write-authority evidence that is absent here.

verified_dimensions.sink: pickle.loads on schedule fields before actor send

responses.rationale: The call is console.log with a JavaScript template literal already interpolated, plus a second data argument. That is not a printf-style format string where an attacker supplies the format. Even without knowing the origin of method or endpoint, the unsafe-formatstring mechanism is absent.
The path joins occur inside a test-only helper in methods.test.ts used to stage mock budget files. The packet shows no production request path or remote attacker interface that invokes this helper.

Requested static paths are normalized and resolved and compared against the resolved client-build root; paths outside that root receive HTTP 403 before net.fetch. The shown control blocks directory traversal out of the client-build tree.
The path.join for a mock budget directory lives only in the methods.test.ts test helper. No production exposure is shown in the packet.

res.send(fileAccessError) is a direct response write on the 403 path. Whether that is XSS depends on whether fileAccessError contains attacker-controlled HTML or JavaScript and on content type. Construction of the error and the response content type are not in the packet, so the XSS claim cannot be confirmed or dismissed.
